title: A New Definition of Quantum Superposition
abstract: The usual description of the superposition of two (pure quantum) states is ambiguous, since the binary operation of summation in a Hilbert space does not pass down to the quotient projective space. Even though Dirac noted this as early as 1930, it is often asserted that the superposition is a binary operation acting on two states with a value that is a unique state. The goal for this note is to motivate a rigorous, geometrical definition of the superposition of states in the setting of complex projective space, which has been argued elsewhere to be the natural geometric phase space for quantum theory. The upshot is that the new definition of the superposition of two pure states, viewed as two distinct points in the projective space, is the unique (complex) line on which those two points lie. Finally, a comparison is given between superposition and expansion in an orthonormal basis.
summary: This paper addresses the ambiguity in defining quantum superposition by reformulating it geometrically within complex projective space. It proposes that the superposition of two states is uniquely defined as the straight line connecting them in this geometric space. This provides a rigorous mathematical foundation independent of traditional summation rules.
main_problem: The standard description of quantum superposition is mathematically ambiguous because the summation operation used in Hilbert space does not translate cleanly to the quotient projective space ($	ext{CP}(H)$).
main_result: A rigorous, geometrical definition of superposition is proposed: it is defined as the unique complex line passing through two distinct pure states viewed as points in $	ext{CP}(H)$.
method: The paper develops a geometric framework by treating quantum states as points in complex projective space and defining superposition based on collinearity axioms.
model_or_system: The model uses pure quantum states, represented geometrically as points in the complex projective space $	ext{CP}(H)$, where $H$ is a complex Hilbert space. The analysis compares this geometric definition to standard basis expansions.
key_observables: Superposition itself (defined as a line/subspace), and the comparison between superposition and classical statistical mixtures derived from orthonormal basis expansions.
important_parameters: The structure of the underlying Hilbert space $H$ and its associated projective geometry $	ext{CP}(H)$.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that viewing quantum states as points in $	ext{CP}(H)$ provides a natural geometric setting, and the definition relies on properties analogous to those found in complex projective geometry.
paper_structure: The paper first identifies the ambiguity of superposition in $	ext{CP}(H)$, then proposes the line-based geometric definition for two states. It subsequently contrasts this with basis expansion and discusses generalizations to other mathematical spaces.
why_interesting: This work provides a fundamental, purely geometrical reinterpretation of one of quantum mechanics' most basic concepts, potentially offering insights applicable beyond standard Hilbert space formalism.
